question: A 30-year-old woman with secondary infertility has an HSG showing bilateral proximal occlusion. A selective salpingography is then performed and demonstrates that the left tube is patent after flushing (spasm relieved), but the right tube remains occluded. What is the most appropriate next step?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Repeating the HSG would not add therapeutic benefit once selective salpingography has confirmed true right-sided proximal occlusion. A diagnostic and therapeutic step is now needed.

answers.text: Proceed directly to IVF without further tubal assessment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: IVF may ultimately be needed, but the patient has one patent tube, and a laparoscopic assessment should first confirm the nature and extent of right-sided disease before bypassing it entirely.

Correct. Laparoscopy with chromopertubation (methylene blue) is the gold standard — it simultaneously confirms the site and severity of obstruction and allows surgical correction (salpingolysis, tuboplasty) where feasible.
Hysteroscopy evaluates the uterine cavity but cannot assess tubal patency or treat peritubal disease. Laparoscopy is the correct modality for confirmed tubal occlusion.

overallFeedback.feedback: For confirmed tubal occlusion (right tube, spasm excluded by selective salpingography), laparoscopy with chromopertubation is the gold standard — it confirms the lesion and allows surgical correction in the same sitting.
Excellent. Laparoscopy with chromopertubation is the gold standard for confirmed tubal disease — it is diagnostic and therapeutic simultaneously.
